result:
If I could change one thing, I think I'd want people to have an easier time extending good faith to those who see the world differently than they do—across political lines, cultural backgrounds, religions, whatever the divide happens to be.

I keep coming back to this one because so many other problems seem downstream of it. Conflicts that could be resolved through cooperation instead calcify because people assume the worst about each other's motives. Solvable disagreements turn into identity battles. Even when people agree on facts, they often can't agree on what to do because they've stopped believing the other side is acting in good faith at all.

I don't mean naive agreeableness, or pretending all positions are equally valid, or refusing to set boundaries with people who are actually acting in bad faith. I mean something more like: a default assumption that the person in front of you is trying to navigate a confusing world as best they can, even when their conclusions seem wrong to you.

That said, I hold this somewhat loosely. I'm aware it might be a generic, low-stakes answer—the kind of thing that sounds nice but avoids harder tradeoffs. A world with less material scarcity, or one where everyone had their basic needs met, might do more concrete good. I'm genuinely unsure how to weigh "fix the material conditions" against "fix how people relate to each other," and I suspect they're tangled together anyway.

What pulled you toward asking the question? I'm curious whether you have a answer of your own that this is testing against.
